title: “If You Don’t Own Your Model, the Model Owns You!” Sovereign AI: What Does It Mean for a Model to Be Sovereign and Is AI Sovereignty a CIO Pipe Dream? – Part 1
excerpt: Two weeks in, Beyond Beta has crossed 1,100 subscribers — and the topic readers ask about most is sovereign AI. Policymakers and business leaders use the term to mean very different things: Ursula von der Leyen calls it the goal for Europe, while two European CIOs call it a complete pipe dream. This briefing starts mapping the fault lines — from CIOs’ fears of data and IP leakage to the East–West divide over whether sovereignty is a compliance exercise or a business opportunity — ahead of a deeper dive to come.
body:
If you are the **CIO of a multi-national company** – and we are thrilled that there are actually quite a lot of you here! – or if you are **leading an AI Center of Excellence**, or, indeed, if you are leading a country and your boss is at the UN Security Council this week, [attending tomorrow’s AI briefing by Sam Altman](https://www.euractiv.com/news/openais-sam-altman-to-brief-un-security-council-next-week/), then stay tuned: **this Beyond Beta briefing is particularly relevant for you!** It will start structuring for you the topic that we got by far the most questions on over the past two weeks: **sovereign AI.**

But first: THANK YOU from Frankfurt, where I am making a brief stopover this week! Two weeks ago we started the Beyond Beta-Briefings [in Oxford](https://lnkd.in/p/dmyVZy6m). **Today we cracked the threshold of 1100 subscribers and counting!** And the sheer number of readers is not the only thing the team and I are excited about: **the briefings are only the publicly visible part of this research project. At the heart of the project is **[**our market analysis of the sovereign tech market, our network analysis, and the comprehensive database and map of AI and tech sovereignty companies, investments, innovators, and products **](index.html)**across Europe and – by popular demand – now also selected other parts of the world **(to the many Middle East and Asian readers and contributors: we are caving in to you!). And for that heart of the project, I received tremendous input from you behind the scenes – thanks a lot!

Our guiding questions for the project are still: Who are the enterprise-scale suppliers of sovereign tech? Who really buys sovereign tech, how do multi-national companies implement it, to what effect, and if so – how much will they spend and how sovereign is sovereign enough for them? If you would like to contribute – any time!

**In the past two weeks, one thing has become unquestionably clear to me: the tech sovereignty market, both the supply and the demand side, is booming. **

That was not necessarily what I expected. Tech sovereignty – a perfect panel discussion and policy bubble topic: for sure! But I was not so certain if there was actually movement in the practical, multi-national, and shareholder-focused realm of CEOs and CIOs. In the past two weeks, **the exponential growth of our market data master spreadsheet and the many contributors that have reached out, agreed to give interviews, help with data, product names, and/or real-life experiences, has astonished me.** If we as a team have not got back to you – we will!

But now on to this week’s topic du jour: sovereign AI. And let me make two things clear upfront: first, if I wanted to spend the rest of my research journey only on this topic, it would be easy to fill the next eight weeks with nothing else.

Second, there is yet again a huge tension between what policymakers mean with the term “Sovereign AI” and what guides their actions, and what business leaders mean with the term and what they are hoping for. While Ursula von der Leyen only last week gave out AI sovereignty as *the* goal for Europe in her State of the Union speech, we spoke also last week with two CIOs of European companies who both proclaimed AI sovereignty was a complete “pipe dream”, totally unachievable. [At the same time, both belong to the 93% of companies that would prefer a German (sovereign!) AI provider, if possible, according to bitkom.](https://www.bitkom.org/Bitkom-Dataverse) What do others here think?

So while it is not possible to tackle the topic in one briefing, let’s use this week to map the issue a bit better. That alone is complex. As with all layers of sovereignty, the deeper I dug into the topic, the easier it was to get completely lost: first, there is indeed no real definition of sovereign AI – policymakers around the world use it in a dozen different ways. [The best summary of this comes from Stanford HAI: “‘Harder’ notions of AI sovereignty emphasize achieving self-sufficiency by ensuring that your country’s ](https://hai.stanford.edu/news/ai-sovereigntys-definitional-dilemma)[AI stack is made up entirely of domestic components](https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/the-dangers-of-ai-sovereignty)[;”, say Caroline Meinhardt and her co-authors, “‘softer’ notions frame sovereignty as strategic autonomy, where governments retain some limited degree of strategic control and regulatory leverage over their AI dependencies. The former is costly and, for the most part, unfeasible for most countries; the latter preserves flexibility but may lead to a false sense of security as AI vendors ultimately retain strategic leverage.”](https://hai.stanford.edu/news/ai-sovereigntys-definitional-dilemma)

**On the tech and business leader side, definitions are equally fuzzy. But what is pretty clear are the fears that CIOs and CEOs have. Most of them hope, sovereign AI will resolve these fears for them**: in Beyond Beta interviews, some CIOs shared with me their fears of data and IP leakage ([**for 45% of companies this is still a main blocker to AI usage overall, according to bitkom**](https://www.bitkom.org/Bitkom-Dataverse/KIUnternehmen?tab_name=Unternehmensinterne+Hemmnisse+beim+Einsatz)). Other CIOs and CEOs complain about what they consider meaningless legal texts that are supposed to protect them from **vendor lock-in, from the “kill switch” of the US or Chinese governments, or from model providers changing the underlying model weights from one day to the next**. Other business leaders point to complex dependencies of all layers of the sovereignty model. For example, does AI sovereignty start on the model, the data, or the application layer or even before? What about the physical hardware, like Chips and [**submarine cables**](https://www.reuters.com/world/europe/nato-allies-foil-russian-subsea-cable-sabotage-plot-2026-09-10/)? So the set of worries on the business side is broad.

In addition, there is an East – West divide in Europe. Western European companies see sovereignty mainly as a compliance exercise or an exercise of business continuity. Eastern European companies go beyond that: [more than 30% of them see sovereignty as a business opportunity.](https://www.bcg.com/publications/2026/germany-how-ai-sovereignty-is-reshaping-europes-technology-strategy?utm_source=linkedin&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=tech_ai&utm_description=organic&utm_topic=digital_sovereignty&utm_geo=ce&utm_content=kr) For example, to get ready to become a supplier for defense companies.

[**“If you don’t own your model, the model owns you”, states Jakob Foerster, Oxford Professor, Senior Tech Lead at Meta AI, and Troublemaker in Chief from the **](https://x.com/j_foerst/status/2097303600221335631?s=43&t=SeCFvqnFfWEdo6UljulZmQ)[**British Open-ended Learning & Discovery Lab**](https://bold-lab.ai/)**.** We will hear from Jakob again in more detail in a forthcoming Beyond Beta Briefing.

For now, we would love to keep collecting more questions on AI sovereignty, especially from the business side. What would you like us to dig deeper into? What have we overlooked so far?

As always, ping us! Follow us along on [www.beyondbeta.eu](index.html) and [sign up for our newsletter](index.html#subscribe) here or – for free and more in-depth content – directly on our website!

title: The Disconnect Between Politics and CEOs on Tech Sovereignty Could Let the Entire Vision Fail
excerpt: The political vision of tech sovereignty could very well fail in the short-range arena of business reality. This tension between CEOs and policymakers is why we have started BeyondBeta.eu. In weekly Briefings and daily Signals coming out of our research project we will research, map, and profile the market and the business leaders, the innovators, the investors, and the policymakers who turn the political vision of Tech and AI Sovereignty into a business reality. The goal is to build a comprehensive database and landscape map of the business side of European Tech and AI sovereignty.
body:
“This whole sovereignty narrative in Europe is dangerous,” says Ericsson CEO Börje Ekholm in an [interview with Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-01-20/ericsson-ceo-says-europe-s-tech-sovereignty-push-is-dangerous?in_source=onboarding_confirmation&source=onboarding_confirmation). In Europe, the topic of sovereignty can be “very emotional — maybe too emotional,” [states SAP CEO Christian Klein](https://www.computerworld.com/article/4121625/european-tech-leaders-advise-caution-on-tech-sovereignty-drive.html). Håkan Samuelsson, CEO of Volvo Cars, tells the FT that [“Europe would be the only loser”](https://www.ft.com/content/3b9c9683-f137-4459-adc9-3679b8899c07?accessToken=zwAAAaCFccFpkc87nJaD8TdEWdOtyTZ5uImcBw.MEUCIQCeMflD9jdRWbHQmIeyOEQazpaUXKH7vhWOECbO9UetigIgeu-OWOkzwOVGd-NhXFYO-citif6oU391oXKoXo7lZyQ&sharetype=gift&token=5ad8d6ec-1d13-489e-a033-150f878ca2a1&syn-25a6b1a6=1) if the EU were to impose any restrictions or barriers on US technology. Ned Curic, chief technology officer of Stellantis, says “it will drive expenses for us and . . . it will eventually drive shrinking of the markets” for Europe’s car industry. Lastly, this single sentence by [Tim Höttges, CEO of Deutsche Telekom](https://www.handelsblatt.com/technik/it-internet/rechenzentren-konzerne-stellen-gigafactorys-infrage-und-kritisieren-eu/100229255.html), is perhaps the most clear-eyed summary of Europe’s current tech sovereignty dilemma. „Deutsche Telekom does not need an AI Gigafactory - Germany needs an AI Gigafactory!“

These quotes by some of Europe’s most important **CEOs crystallize the tension and the many misunderstandings between European business leaders and political leaders when it comes to shaping Europe’s tech strategy** vis-à-vis China and the USA. Tech sovereignty may be politically vital for Europe. But for multi-national companies, it is more than a challenging business case and ultimately a bet that may not pay off.

The political vision of tech sovereignty could very well fail in the short-range arena of business reality.

**This tension between CEOs and policymakers is why we have started** **[BeyondBeta.eu](index.html).** In weekly Briefings and daily Signals coming out of our research project we will research, map, and profile the market and the business leaders, the innovators, the investors, and the policymakers who turn the political vision of Tech and AI Sovereignty into a business reality. **The goal is to build a comprehensive database and landscape map of the business side of European Tech and AI sovereignty.**

On the one hand, on the political side, there is no shortage of rallying to action for the buzzword of tech sovereignty. Presidents and Heads of State use it in every speech, strategy papers amount to a dozen per day, even hard EU regulation, [like the Cloud and AI Development Act](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/cloud-and-ai-development-act), is under way. High-profile summit meetings, like the [German-French summit in Berlin last November](https://www.bundesregierung.de/breg-en/news/digital-sovereignty-2394992), or the upcoming AI summit in Dublin in a few weeks aim to create more momentum for the political vision, even if that vision is still somewhat blurry.

On the other side, on the side of **business leaders, investors, and scale-ups founders, CEOs struggle to turn that vision into a business reality** – or, indeed, may not have high on the agenda to support it. They are measured by short-term P&L success, not civic duty. That includes hard numbers on cost effectiveness, capacity for innovation, the ease and speed of tech and AI implementation in multi-national production environments. Sovereign products, like sovereign cloud or European AI models, can provide little of that. They cost about 20+% more than their US competitors and they are, frankly, clunky to use. In addition, particularly multi-nationals cannot find themselves on the wrong side of either China or the USA. Going sovereign can be seen as the wrong signal. It also does not help that some businesses have already been through politically motivated tech projects, that proved nothing but painful and costly. [GAIA-X](https://gaia-x.eu/), for example, or FCAS.

**For me personally, the debate on Europe’s tech sovereignty started more than five years ago in 2021 in the office of German Chancellor Angela Merkel.** With just a handful of her policy advisors, the Chancellor went over the final draft of an [open letter that she was about to send to Ursula von der Leyen, the President of the European Commission](https://www.handelsblatt.com/meinung/gastbeitraege/digitalisierung-appell-von-vier-regierungschefinnen-an-die-eu-europa-muss-seine-digitale-souveraenitaet-staerken/26962398.html). Together with Kaja Kallas, Mette Frederiksen and Sanna Marin Angela Merkel put the topic of tech sovereignty on the political agenda that day. Ever since, the subject has never left my career or the political agenda again.

Going from policymaker, where we negotiated tough sovereignty questions such as broken chips supply chains and Huawei’s role in the 5G toolbox, to being an academic, to now as a [management consultant supporting multi-national clients](https://www.linkedin.com/in/kirstenrulf/). The tech sovereignty topic has only ever gained importance.

That is why, over the months ahead, my team and I are driving “Beyond Beta”.

**“Beyond Beta” exists because debates about tech sovereignty are currently often confined to the policy bubble and too seldom connect the political ambition of tech sovereignty with the practical, multi-national, and shareholder-focused perspective of CEOs and CIOs.**

This disconnect constrains both the supply side of tech sovereignty, i.e. the companies and startups that develop and sell sovereign products. And it deters those that are supposed to buy or invest in sovereign products, i.e. the demand side. Neither side knows what the market really looks like and if their (expensive) bet on sovereignty will pay off. Who really buys sovereign tech and if so – how much will they spend and how sovereign is sovereign enough for them? Will regulation, like the EU Cloud and Development Act, really come, or will it be too late and anyways not precise enough to calculate a total addressable market? Besides, will governments really stay true to becoming lead customers for sovereignty providers?

**So what can you expect from** **[“Beyond Beta”](index.html) and why should you sign up for our briefings?**

You will get to know the companies, innovators, and investors actively working to turn digital sovereignty from a political vision and buzzword into entrepreneurial reality. You will also gain insights into markets, political milestones, considerations, and key decision-makers shaping the framework conditions. And you will receive context and analysis of current events.

The result of our research project is a comprehensive database and map of AI and tech sovereignty companies, investments, and products across Europe and other parts of the world. “Beyond Beta” aims to provide market orientation, highlight potential solutions from less obvious players, and put curated tools, frameworks, and playbooks to the test.

And it aims to anticipate the headlines. Given I am still as much a policy wonk as a businessperson I know what still lies ahead of us: in a few weeks, politicians, defense, automotive, and the energy CEOs will be hotly debating Rare Earth supplies from China; in a few months, [as the EU Commission confirms](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/europe-advance-6g-innovation-20-projects-set-receive-eu116-million), we will be discussing 6G and OpenRAN. All the time, AI and cybersecurity will dominate the news, and the question whether Europe and the rest of the world will still have access to the latest Frontier AI models.

How does “Beyond Beta” tackle the topic?

First, we offer our weekly “Beyond Beta” briefings. Short background analysis, readable in under 10 minutes, that reports on highlights from our journey across Europe and beyond. People, products, markets that you need to know about beyond the daily headlines to help you make strategic decisions or simply stay up to date in the global sovereign debate. In addition, we offer daily “signals” – a comprehensive overview with everything you need to know that is happening across all eight layers of the tech stack. Business updates, news headlines, political milestones, academic analysis, all in one place, searchable.

**We look forward to this journey with you – see you next Tuesday for the next Beyond Beta Briefing?**

title: “This Is Not Investing for Sissies!”
excerpt: In about 8 weeks, China will impose export controls on rare earths, semiconductors, superhard materials, and lithium batteries — and European production will feel it fast. But Europe’s CEOs are far from done fighting: Solvay, Schaeffler, BMW, and others are already investing directly in new REE mines, and Renault, BMW, and Mahle are racing to build REE-free components. As Henk de Hoop of SFA Oxford puts it, investing in the mining industry is relatively high risk, and not for sissies.
body:
In about 8 weeks, China will pull the plug on a critical part of the supply chain for defense companies, for energy, for automotive companies, for AI data centers, and for manufacturing. **In Mid-November, as announced a year ago,** **[it will impose export controls on products, equipment, and technologies related to rare earth elements, on semiconductors, on superhard materials, and lithium batteries, among others.](https://www.whitecase.com/insight-alert/china-imposes-extraterritorial-jurisdiction-and-50-rule-export-controls-rare-earth)** **Production in Europe will halt, prices are already going through the roof, European companies will lose billion Euros in revenue,** [as the European Central Bank estimates.](https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/economic-bulletin/articles/2025/html/ecb.ebart202505_01~c93c71e372.en.html) **Politicians and CEOs will talk about little else in the winter months.** *"We have sharply increased inquiries based on the most recent "blacklist" that China has sent out, where **they named 14 European companies, including defense companies, that will not be able to have access to their niche metals or materials anymore**"*, says Henk de Hoop, when I met him for our [BeyondBeta-interview](index.html). De Hoop has been one of Europe's principal industry experts on Critical Raw Materials. For nearly 30 years he has been working in both mining engineering and mining finance. He has himself worked in mines in South Africa as an engineer. **Today Henk de Hoop is** **[CEO of SFA Oxford](https://www.sfa-oxford.com/), which delivers highly specialized market analysis and advises business and political leaders globally on their REE strategy***.* *"It is already happening today in real time that some companies are shut out of metals or components, e.g. dual use components, because China has put its foot down."*

**And yet, I initially thought that this Layer Zero of sovereignty hardly deserved our attention. "Beyond Beta" aims to be solution-oriented, not problem-admiring.** And with Rare Earth Elements (REE) and Critical Raw Materials, it is a truism, that Europe and the rest of the world is fully depended on Chinese exports and refinement, and that there is nothing that can be done about it.

**What a mistake! Critical Raw Materials is a layer of sovereignty where Europe's CEOs are for sure not done fighting. Far from it!**

Did you know that **[Solvay, Schaeffler, BMW, and tk accelis GmbH (until June thyssenkrupp Materials Services GmbH), are some of the largest investors in actual new REE mines around the world?](https://dip.bundestag.de/vorgang/bericht-des-ausschusses-f%C3%BCr-forschung-technologie-raumfahrt-und-technikfolgenabsch%C3%A4tzung-18/334689)** Have you heard about a chemical called P507 that is crucial to mine REE and that few companies other than BASF and Solvay can produce economically? Which makes it **a suitable geopolitical bargaining chip**, of course. Besides, Europe is driving innovation: **Renault, BMW, and Mahle are frontrunners in REE-free car components.**

When it comes to REE and sovereignty, European CEOs of manufacturing giants to automotive companies, the demand side of the market, is newly pushing into all stages of the supply side. **Some of** **these CEOs, investors and experts agree, are perhaps making too unprecedented and daring strategic moves in a highly political territory that is unknown to them**: *"Lots of money has been burned in failed mining projects, even by very reputable big companies like Rio Tinto, BHP, Anglo-American",* says Henk de Hoop in our interview. *"They all have scars of billion-dollar losses because they, even with all their decades of professionalism and experience applied, overlooked or missed something critical, causing the overall project to become uneconomic or inexecutable. **So, investing in the mining industry is relatively high risk and not for sissies."***

**As the weeks tick down until the Chinese ultimatum runs out,** **we will periodically brief you in episodes of our newsletter and bring you up to the mark before the story hits the headlines.** Already the global debate is simmering, and we add a new article on Rare Earth Elements (REE) to our [“signals” section almost every day](index.html). **And yet again we will encounter the question, if and why the policy response is so disconnected to what CEOs are trying to do -- and how that could change.**

Our research on REE and sovereignty led us to **Narva in Estonia**, a town from where you can walk across the Russian boarder in under 20 minutes. Here the EU let Canada build a highly strategic company, giving millions of Euros in subsidies and a building permission within only weeks. The journey will lead us to Bitterfeld in East Germany and **Heraeus' unique REE recycling technology plant** there. We will introduce you to the **frontline innovators in the Critical Raw Materials space, to the R&D labs, where engineers claim to be the frontrunners in developing products with far fewer REE.** We will visit edge innovators like the Oxford University startup which develops technology to extract critical minerals and REE from volcanic rock and underground geothermal brines, and the University of Vienna research group that investigates "mycomining", a technique that uses fungi and mushrooms to extract REE from industrial waste and contaminated soils. **And of course, we stopped at Brussels and the German Bundestag.**

However, we will start with a full interview with Henk de Hoop on www.BeyondBeta.eu, covering **an overview of the entire supply chain of Critical Raw Materials, the strategic steps that demand-side CEOs can make, who are not as audacious or deep-pocketed,** and with de Hoop's perspective on REE recycling and the efforts of the EU Critical Raw Materials Act on that front.

Can European companies and politicians succeed in jointly crafting at least some geopolitical bargaining chips on Sovereignty Layer Zero? Or is it too little too late? Not necessarily, says expert de Hoop. However, there will be heavy losses. **"But sometimes that is the price to pay. Rather than not producing anything, because you do not have the access anymore to the particular REE that you need."** 

Read more later this week on [www.BeyondBeta.eu](index.html)
